draft.title: Challenges to democracy
card: After World War I, many European states became democracies, with elected governments and written constitutions. Many were new and had little experience of democratic rule.
Economic crisis
inflation, debt and unemployment left many people poor and angry. Voters often blamed the government and looked for a stronger alternative.
Political violence
armed groups and street fighting, often between the far left and far right, made governments look weak and unable to keep order.
Distrust

many people doubted that elected politicians could solve problems. Some saw democracy as slow and divided. Between the wars, many states gave way to authoritarian rule, where one leader or party held power without real checks.
draft.remember: Hardship, violence and distrust weakened new democracies, and many turned to authoritarian rule.

a.q: Why were new democracies in interwar Europe often easy to undermine?
opts: Hardship, violence and distrust weakened faith in them
They had no elections or written constitutions
They were ruled by a single party from the start
Their citizens had long experience of self-government
a.why: Economic crisis, political violence and distrust made governments look weak, so many people were open to stronger leaders. The second option is wrong because these states did hold elections and had constitutions.
a.clue: Think about what made people lose faith in elected governments.

b.q: In a new democracy, street fights between rival armed groups become common and unemployment is high. Many voters say, "Parliament cannot keep order." What is the most likely effect?
opts: Support may grow for a leader promising strong rule
Voters will trust parliament more than before
Armed groups will become the lawful government
The economy will recover because order returns
b.why: Violence and hardship can make parliament look weak, so some voters may turn to a leader who promises order. Trusting parliament more is wrong because the scenario describes distrust growing, not shrinking.
b.clue: Ask what people want when they think the government is weak.

a.best: Hardship, violence and distrust weakened faith in them

b.best: Support may grow for a leader promising strong rule

problems.detail: Why (a) calls the 'no elections or written constitutions' option 'the second option'. Options are shown in random order, and here the second option is the correct answer, so students would be told the right answer is wrong. Name the option by its content instead of its position.

check.summary: The card and both questions are accurate and each has one clear answer. Why (a) refers to a distractor as 'the second option', which in the shuffled order points to the correct answer and should name the option by its content.
